Singular value decomposition with optional scaling and truncation

Source: R/fs_svd.R
fs_svd.Rd

Computes the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a numeric matrix, optionally centering and scaling it first and keeping only the leading singular values and vectors. The SVD factors a matrix into u %*% diag(d) %*% t(v); the leading terms give the best low-rank approximation of the matrix in the least-squares sense.

Usage

fs_svd(
  x,
  n_singular_values = NULL,
  scale_input = TRUE,
  svd_method = c("auto", "exact", "approx"),
  svd_threshold = 100,
  approx_args = list(),
  verbose = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

Numeric matrix, or a data.frame whose columns are all numeric (it is coerced to a matrix). It must contain no NA, NaN, or Inf values. The argument is called x rather than data because it is a matrix of values, not a table of observations and features.

n_singular_values

Positive whole number of singular values and vectors to keep, or NULL (default) for min(dim(x)). A value above min(dim(x)) is an error.

scale_input

How to transform the columns before decomposing: TRUE (default) centers and scales, FALSE leaves the matrix alone, "center" subtracts column means only, and "scale" divides only. Any other value is an error. The two dividing forms (TRUE and "scale") need every column to have non-zero variance, meaning a standard deviation above 1000 * .Machine$double.eps (about 2e-13) times the column's largest absolute value, so the check does not depend on units. Offending columns are named in the error, or numbered when the matrix has no column names. "scale" follows base::scale(): without centering it divides by the root mean square, not the standard deviation.

svd_method

"auto" (default), "exact", or "approx". See Details for how "auto" decides and when "approx" falls back to the exact solver.

svd_threshold

Positive number. With svd_method = "auto", the approximate solver is considered only when min(dim(x)) exceeds it. Default 100.

approx_args

List of extra arguments passed to RSpectra::svds(), for example tol or opts. It must not include A or k, which are set from x and n_singular_values.

verbose

Logical; print progress messages. Default FALSE.

Value

A plain list, not an fs_result: fs_svd() reduces dimensions rather than selecting features. Writing k for the number kept (n_singular_values, or min(dim(x)) by default), the components are:

  • singular_values: numeric vector of length k, in non-increasing order.

  • left_singular_vectors: nrow(x) by k matrix (the u of base::svd()).

  • right_singular_vectors: ncol(x) by k matrix (the v of base::svd()).

Singular vectors are unique only up to sign (and up to rotation within a block of tied singular values), so column signs can differ between the exact and approximate solvers and between platforms.

Details

Use it for a low-rank summary of a numeric matrix: compression, denoising, or a latent-factor representation. The components are linear combinations of every input column, so nothing is dropped and the components cannot be read as individual features; use one of featR's selection functions when you need to name the features you keep. fs_pca() covers the same ground with labeled output and variance-explained figures; fs_svd() is the lower-level decomposition.

The exact solver is base::svd(). The approximate solver is RSpectra::svds() (from RSpectra, a Suggests dependency needed only when that solver runs), and it can only return fewer than min(dim(x)) singular values. The default n_singular_values = NULL asks for all min(dim(x)) of them and so always takes the exact path; request fewer to make the approximate solver available.

With svd_method = "auto", the approximate solver runs only when n_singular_values < min(dim(x)) and min(dim(x)) > svd_threshold. Otherwise the exact solver runs, and a message explains why when a large matrix ends up on the exact path because all singular values were requested. svd_method = "approx" with n_singular_values equal to min(dim(x)) is not an error: it falls back to the exact solver with a message. If RSpectra::svds() converges on fewer singular values than requested, the call warns and recomputes them with the exact solver.

Centering and scaling happen before the decomposition, so the returned values and vectors factorize the transformed matrix. With the default scale_input = TRUE they reconstruct scale(x), not x. The column means and standard deviations are not returned; keep them yourself if you need to map results back to the original units.

See also

The Dimensionality reduction guide, which runs this function on a worked example.

Examples

m <- matrix(
  c(4, 0, 0, 3,
    0, 5, 1, 2,
    2, 1, 6, 0,
    1, 3, 2, 7,
    5, 2, 0, 1,
    0, 4, 3, 2),
  nrow = 6, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE
)

# Two leading components of the centered and scaled matrix
res <- fs_svd(m, n_singular_values = 2, scale_input = TRUE)
res$singular_values
#> [1] 3.075623 2.574852
res$left_singular_vectors
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.5433794 -0.2618208
#> [2,]  0.4467209 -0.1147094
#> [3,] -0.1104811  0.8100647
#> [4,]  0.2986167 -0.4626424
#> [5,] -0.4927382 -0.1397594
#> [6,]  0.4012610  0.1688673
res$right_singular_vectors
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.7067452 -0.1089774
#> [2,]  0.6323538 -0.1568284
#> [3,]  0.2259715  0.7369407
#> [4,]  0.2226583 -0.6484190

# Share of the total (scaled) variance captured by those two components
all_values <- fs_svd(m, scale_input = TRUE)$singular_values
sum(res$singular_values^2) / sum(all_values^2)
#> [1] 0.804466

# Untransformed, the full decomposition reconstructs the input exactly
full <- fs_svd(m, scale_input = FALSE)
recon <- full$left_singular_vectors %*%
  (full$singular_values * t(full$right_singular_vectors))
all.equal(recon, m)
#> [1] TRUE
